title: Raft and Paxos consensus
summary: How replicas agree on one log despite crashes: majority quorums, Paxos prepare and accept, Raft elections, log replication and its safety rules, and how production systems serve reads and change membership.
outcomes: Explain why any two majorities overlap and how many failures a cluster of n servers tolerates
Trace a Paxos run and say which value a proposer must propose after phase 1
Walk through a Raft election and explain why randomized timeouts prevent repeated split votes
Compute a Raft leader's commitIndex from matchIndex values and spot the older-term commit trap
Choose between ReadIndex and lease reads and explain why membership changes go one server at a time

lessons.title: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work

blocks.md:
From the consistency models course you know the goal: a replicated service that looks **linearizable**, as if one copy executed each operation at a single instant. The standard way to build that is a **replicated state machine**: every server keeps a **log** (an ordered list of commands) and feeds it to a deterministic **state machine**. If every log holds the same commands in the same order, every replica computes the same state and the same outputs.

Keeping those logs identical while servers crash and messages get lost is the job of a **consensus algorithm**. This course covers the two you will meet most: Paxos and Raft.

blocks.title: A replicated state machine on three servers

scenes.caption: Each server has three parts: a consensus module, a log of commands, and a deterministic state machine (for example a key-value map). A client sends the command SET x=5 to the server acting as leader.
The consensus module appends the command to its own log and sends it to the other servers, which append it to theirs. The goal: every log holds the same commands in the same order.
Once the entry is safely stored on a majority it is committed, and each server applies it to its state machine in log order. Same inputs in the same order give the same state everywhere.
If S3 crashes, S1 and S2 are still a majority (2 of 3), so the cluster keeps accepting commands. When S3 comes back, the leader brings its log up to date.

blocks.md:
Why not something simpler?

- **One server.** It is consistent, but when it fails the service stops (Lamport opens Paxos Made Simple with exactly this single acceptor and rejects it for this reason).
- **Write to every replica.** Safe, but one crashed replica blocks every write.
- **Primary plus backup with a failover timeout.** The backup cannot tell a crashed primary from a slow network. If it takes over while the old primary is alive but cut off, both accept writes.

blocks.prompt: A primary and its backup lose contact. After 3 seconds the backup promotes itself. The old primary was not dead: a switch had failed and two clients can still reach it. What happens to the data?
blocks.reveal: You get **split brain**: two primaries each accept writes that the other never sees, so the replicas diverge and no ordering of the two histories is linearizable. A timeout can only *suspect* a failure, never prove one. A correct protocol must stay safe even when its failure guesses are wrong.

blocks.md: The fix used by both Paxos and Raft is the **majority quorum**: a decision counts only once more than half of the servers have recorded it. Any two majorities of the same set share at least one server, so two conflicting decisions can never both collect a majority. That shared server acts as a witness that carries information from one decision to the next.

blocks.caption: Quorum size q and failures tolerated f for n servers. Two quorums overlap because 2q > n. The last equation is the smallest cluster that tolerates f failures; it holds only for odd n.

blocks.title: Majority size and failures tolerated by cluster size

scenes.caption: Majority (quorum) size $q = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$. Every decision needs this many servers to answer, so q grows by one every two servers.
Failures tolerated $f = n - q$: the cluster keeps working as long as a majority is up. Going from 3 to 4 or from 5 to 6 servers adds cost but no extra fault tolerance.

blocks.md: An even cluster is not more fault tolerant than the odd one below it. Four servers need 3 for a majority and still survive only 1 failure, and a 2 to 2 network split leaves neither side able to decide. The Raft paper calls five servers typical: it tolerates two failures.

The model both algorithms assume (Lamport states it explicitly): servers may run at any speed, crash, and restart with their stable storage intact; messages may be delayed, duplicated, or lost, but not corrupted. There are no malicious (Byzantine) servers.

In that model, safety must never depend on timing. Timeouts are allowed to decide only *liveness*, meaning whether the system makes progress. Lamport notes that, by the Fischer, Lynch and Paterson impossibility result, reliably electing a leader needs randomness or real time such as timeouts.
Majorities intersect. Every safety argument in Paxos and Raft comes down to one server that sat in both quorums and remembered what it saw.

blocks.question: A 5-server cluster is split by a network failure into a group of 2 servers and a group of 3. Which side can still commit new commands?
options: Both sides, and they reconcile later
Only the side with 3 servers
Only the side that holds the current leader
Neither side until the network heals
blocks.explain: Committing needs a majority of the full cluster, which is 3 of 5. Only the 3-server side has one. If the old leader is on the 2-server side, it can keep accepting requests but can never commit them; the 3-server side elects a new leader and keeps going.

blocks.question: You run a 3-server cluster and add a fourth server for extra safety. How many simultaneous server failures can the cluster now survive while staying available?
options: 1, the same as before
2, one more than before
3, since one server is enough to serve reads
0, because 4 cannot form a majority
blocks.explain: With n = 4 the majority is 3, so only 1 server may be down. You added replication cost (one more copy on every write) without improving availability. Go to 5 servers to tolerate 2 failures.

lessons.title: Paxos: choosing one value with prepare and accept

blocks.md:
Lamport's **Paxos** (described plainly in *Paxos Made Simple*, 2001) first solves a narrower problem: a group must **choose a single value**. The safety rules are: only a proposed value can be chosen, only one value is chosen, and no one learns a value unless it really was chosen.

There are three roles. **Proposers** suggest values, **acceptors** vote on them, and **learners** find out the result. One process usually plays all three. A **proposal** is a pair (number n, value v); proposers draw numbers from disjoint sets so no two proposals share a number. A value is **chosen** when one proposal carrying it has been accepted by a majority of acceptors.

Why two phases? If an acceptor simply accepted the first value it heard, two proposers could split the acceptors and nothing would reach a majority. So acceptors must be able to accept several proposals, and then the danger is that a later proposal carries a different value after one was already chosen.

Lamport's key invariant: **if a proposal with value v is chosen, every higher-numbered proposal that is issued also has value v.** To keep it, a proposer first asks a majority what they have accepted (phase 1, prepare) and extracts a promise that they will not accept anything numbered lower. Only then does it ask them to accept (phase 2).

blocks.title: Single-decree Paxos: a second proposer must adopt X

scenes.caption: Phase 1a. P1 picks proposal number 1 and sends prepare(1) to a majority, A1 and A2. It is asking: promise to ignore anything numbered below 1, and tell me what you already accepted.
Phase 1b. Neither acceptor has accepted anything, so both promise and report none. A majority of promises lets P1 propose any value it likes.
Phase 2a/2b. P1 sends accept(1, X). A1 and A2 accept it. Proposal 1 is now accepted by a majority of 3 acceptors, so the value X is chosen, even though no one has been told yet.
P2 wakes up wanting value Y. It picks a higher number, 2, and sends prepare(2) to A2 and A3, a different majority.
A2 promises but reports that it accepted (1, X). A3 reports none. The two majorities {A1, A2} and {A2, A3} overlap in A2, and A2 carries the news.
The rule forces P2 to propose the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal it heard about, which is X, not its own Y. Proposal 2 is accepted with value X, so the chosen value never changes.
A late accept(1, X) from P1 reaches A3. A3 promised not to accept anything below 2, so it ignores it. Promises are what make old, delayed messages harmless.

blocks.prompt: Pause at the scene where P2 sends prepare(2). P2 wants value Y and has never heard of X. After the promises from A2 and A3 arrive, which value is P2 allowed to propose?
blocks.reveal: **X.** A2's promise reports that it accepted (1, X). The rule says: propose the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal among the promises, and only if none was reported may you pick your own. Because the majority P2 contacted must overlap the majority that chose X, P2 is guaranteed to hear about X.

blocks.title: Acceptor state during the same run

scenes.caption: Each acceptor stores just two things on stable storage: the highest prepare number it has answered, and the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted. All start empty.
After prepare(1): A1 and A2 have promised 1. A3 never heard from P1.
After accept(1, X): A1 and A2 hold 1:X. Two of three acceptors means X is chosen.
After prepare(2): A2 and A3 promise 2. A2 still holds 1:X and reports it in its promise.
After accept(2, X): A2 and A3 hold 2:X. Different proposal numbers, same value. A3 later ignores accept(1, X) because 1 is below its promise of 2.

blocks.caption: An acceptor in single-decree Paxos (Python sketch). Both variables must be written to stable storage before replying.

blocks.md: A Paxos proposer is not free to pick its value. After phase 1 it must adopt the value of the highest-numbered proposal any acceptor in its majority reports. That single rule is what keeps a chosen value from ever changing.

Safety holds no matter how messages are lost or reordered, but **progress is not guaranteed**. Two proposers can keep pre-empting each other with ever higher numbers, as below. Lamport's remedy is to elect one **distinguished proposer** (a leader) that alone issues proposals; the election can use timeouts because a wrong election only costs progress, never safety.

scenes.caption: P1 completes phase 1 with number 1. Before its accept requests arrive, P2 completes phase 1 with number 2.
P1's accept(1) is ignored because acceptors promised 2. P1 retries with prepare(3), which makes P2's accept(2) fail in turn.

The pattern can repeat forever: nothing unsafe happens, but nothing is ever chosen. Simplified: blocks show order, not exact timing; a real duel needs uneven message delays. Lamport's fix is a single distinguished proposer.

blocks.md: **Multi-Paxos** turns this into a replicated log: run one Paxos instance per log slot, with the leader as the only proposer. A new leader runs phase 1 once for all unfinished slots with a single message. After that, each new command needs only phase 2, a single round trip to a majority, which Lamport notes is the minimum possible cost. Because the leader may have several slots in flight, a crash can leave **gaps**, which the next leader fills with no-ops.

blocks.title: Multi-Paxos: a new leader fills the gaps (Lamport's example)

scenes.caption: One Paxos instance per log slot. A new leader knows the commands chosen in instances 1 to 134, 138 and 139. Slots 135 to 137 and 140 onward are unknown to it.
It runs phase 1 for 135 to 137 and every instance above 139 at once, with one short message using one proposal number. Replies pin down values for 135 and 140; the rest are unconstrained.
It runs phase 2 for 135 and 140, and fills 136 and 137 with no-op commands that leave the state unchanged, so 138 to 140 do not wait for future client commands.
Commands 1 to 140 are chosen and can be executed in order. The next client command becomes 141 and needs only phase 2: one round trip to a majority.

blocks.question: An acceptor has promised 5 and has accepted proposal (3, X). It now receives accept(4, Y). What does it do?
options: Accepts (4, Y) because 4 is greater than 3
Replaces its value with Y but keeps number 3
Ignores the request because it promised not to accept anything numbered below 5
Accepts it only if Y equals X
blocks.explain: The acceptor may accept proposal n only if it has not answered a prepare with a number greater than n. It answered prepare(5), so any proposal numbered below 5 is ignored, whatever its value. The comparison is with the promise, not with the last accepted number.

blocks.question: A proposer finished phase 1 with number 7. Promises: A1 accepted (2, X), A2 accepted (4, Y), A3 accepted nothing. Which value must it send in accept(7, ?)
options: X, because it was accepted first
Its own value, because no value had a majority
Either X or Y, whichever it prefers
Y, the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal
blocks.explain: The rule picks the value of the highest-numbered proposal among the replies, here (4, Y). Y might already be chosen through a majority this proposer did not contact; (2, X) was never chosen: if it had been, every higher-numbered proposal issued, including (4, Y), would carry X.

lessons.title: Raft leader election: terms, votes and randomized timeouts

blocks.md: **Raft** (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014) was designed with understandability as the main goal. It splits consensus into three parts: **leader election**, **log replication**, and **safety**. It also uses a *strong leader*: log entries only flow from the leader to the others, and the leader decides where each command goes. Paxos treats leadership as an optimization; in Raft it is part of the protocol.

Time is divided into **terms**, numbered with consecutive integers. Each term starts with an election and has at most one leader. A term acts as a logical clock: every server stores `currentTerm`, every RPC carries the sender's term, and:

- if a server sees a higher term, it adopts it and becomes a follower;
- if it receives a request with a lower term, it rejects it.

Raft needs only two RPCs for its core: **RequestVote** (sent by candidates) and **AppendEntries** (sent by leaders, both to replicate entries and, when empty, as a heartbeat).

scenes.caption: Every server starts as a follower. Followers are passive: they only answer RPCs from leaders and candidates.
If a follower hears nothing from a leader for an election timeout, it becomes a candidate: it increments its term, votes for itself, and asks everyone else for votes.

A candidate with votes from a majority of the full cluster becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats. If its timeout expires with no winner, it stays candidate and starts a new election in a new term.
Any server that sees a higher term in any message adopts that term and becomes a follower. This is how a stale leader or candidate steps down.

blocks.md:
**Election rules.** A follower resets its election timer whenever it gets AppendEntries from the current leader or grants a vote. If the timer expires, it increments `currentTerm`, becomes a candidate, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote to every other server in parallel. Then one of three things happens: it gets votes from a majority and becomes leader; it receives AppendEntries from a leader whose term is at least its own and steps back to follower; or the timeout passes with no winner and it starts another election in the next term.

Each server grants at most one vote per term, first come first served (lesson 5 adds one more condition).

blocks.title: A leader election in a 5-server cluster

scenes.caption: S1, leader of term 1, crashes. Heartbeats stop. Each follower's randomized election timer keeps running.
S3's timer fires first. It increments its term to 2, votes for itself, persists that vote, and sends RequestVote(term 2) to all four others. The one to S1 is lost.
S2 and S4 have not voted in term 2 and S3's log is at least as up to date as theirs, so each grants its vote and resets its own timer. With its own vote S3 has 3 of 5: a majority.
S5's vote arrives later. It changes nothing: S3 already won. At most one server can win term 2, because each server votes once per term and two majorities would need a shared voter.
S3 immediately sends heartbeats (AppendEntries with no entries) to assert its authority and keep the followers' timers from firing.
When S1 restarts, its first contact carries term 2. S1 sees a higher term than its own, adopts term 2, and becomes a follower of S3.

blocks.md: `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and the log must reach stable storage *before* a server answers an RPC. If a server voted, crashed, and forgot its vote, it could vote again in the same term for a different candidate, and two leaders could be elected for one term.

blocks.prompt: With 5 servers and a fixed (not random) election timeout, the leader dies. What usually happens next, and why?
blocks.reveal: All followers last heard the same heartbeat, so their timers expire at nearly the same moment. Several become candidates, each votes for itself, and the votes split so nobody reaches 3. The next election starts in lockstep too, so the split can repeat. **Randomness breaks the symmetry.**

blocks.title: Fixed timeouts split the vote; random ones do not

scenes.caption: Leader S1 dies at t = 0. With the same fixed 150 ms timeout, S2 to S5 all become candidates at once, each votes for itself, and no one reaches 3 votes. The term ends with no leader.
With fixed timeouts the next round fires in lockstep again, so the split can repeat. The Raft authors measured elections taking over 10 seconds with no randomness.
Now each timer is drawn from 150 to 300 ms: here 210, 162, 245 and 281. S3 fires first, and its RequestVotes arrive long before anyone else's timer ends.
S3 wins with 3 votes by about 172 ms and starts heartbeats, which reset the other timers before they fire. Simplified: one round trip assumed to take about 10 ms.

blocks.md: Raft picks each election timeout at random from a fixed interval, for example 150 to 300 ms, and draws a fresh one at the start of each election. Usually one server times out alone, wins, and sends heartbeats before anyone else fires. In the paper's measurements on a 5-server cluster, adding just 5 ms of randomness cut the median downtime to 287 ms; with 50 ms of randomness the worst case over 1000 trials was 513 ms; and with 12 to 24 ms timeouts a leader was elected in 35 ms on average.

blocks.question: Server S2 is a follower with currentTerm 4. It receives RequestVote from S4 for term 3. What does S2 do?
options: Grants the vote if it has not voted yet in term 3
Rejects it and replies with term 4, so S4 learns it is behind
Becomes a candidate for term 5
Adopts term 3 and grants the vote
blocks.explain: Any request with a stale term is rejected, and the reply carries the responder's current term. When S4 sees term 4 it updates its term and returns to follower. Terms never go backward.

blocks.question: Candidate S3 (term 7) is waiting for votes when it receives AppendEntries from S5 claiming to be leader of term 7. What should S3 do?
options: Recognize S5 as leader and return to follower state
Reject it, since S3 started its election first
Increment to term 8 and continue the election
Keep collecting votes; the server with more votes wins
blocks.explain: If the leader's term is at least as large as the candidate's term, the candidate accepts the leader as legitimate and steps down. S5 must already have a majority for term 7, so S3 cannot also win term 7.

lessons.title: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit

blocks.md: Once elected, the leader serves clients. For each command it appends a **log entry** holding the command, the **term** in which the leader received it, and its **index** (position, starting at 1). It then sends AppendEntries to every follower in parallel. An entry is **committed** once the leader that created it has stored it on a majority; committed entries are durable and will eventually be applied by every available state machine. The leader then applies the entry and replies to the client. It keeps retrying followers that did not answer, indefinitely.

blocks.title: Replicating one command in a 3-server cluster

scenes.caption: The client sends SET x=5 to the leader. S1 appends it to its log as entry 4 with term 2. Nothing is committed yet: the entry exists on one server only.
S1 sends AppendEntries to both followers in parallel. Each carries prevLogIndex 3 and prevLogTerm 2 (the index and term of the entry just before the new one), the new entry, and leaderCommit 3.
S2 finds an entry at index 3 with term 2, so the check passes. It appends entry 4, persists it, and replies success. S3's reply is lost in the network.
Entry 4 is now stored on S1 and S2: 2 of 3 is a majority and the entry is from the current term, so S1 sets commitIndex to 4, applies x=5, and answers the client.
The next AppendEntries tells followers leaderCommit 4, so they apply entry 4 too. S1 keeps retrying S3 until it confirms; the retry is harmless because AppendEntries is idempotent.

blocks.md:
Raft keeps logs coherent with the **Log Matching Property**: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, they hold the same command, and they are identical in all earlier entries.

The first half holds because a leader creates at most one entry per index in a term, and entries never move. The second half comes from a **consistency check**: each AppendEntries names the index and term of the entry just before the new ones (`prevLogIndex`, `prevLogTerm`). A follower without a matching entry refuses. By induction, a successful AppendEntries means the follower's log equals the leader's up to the new entries.

Leader crashes can leave followers missing entries, holding extra uncommitted entries, or both. Raft's repair rule is blunt: **the leader forces followers' logs to match its own.** It keeps a `nextIndex` per follower, starting one past its own last entry, and decrements it after each rejection. When the check finally succeeds, the follower deletes everything after the matching point that conflicts and appends the leader's entries. The leader itself never deletes or overwrites its own entries.

blocks.title: Repairing a follower's log by walking nextIndex back

scenes.caption: Numbers are the term of each entry. The follower holds two uncommitted term-2 entries from a leader that crashed. The new leader of term 3 starts with nextIndex = 7, one past its last entry.
AppendEntries with prev = (6, t3): the follower has no entry 6, so it rejects. The leader sets nextIndex to 6.
prev = (5, t3): the follower's entry 5 has term 2, not 3. Reject again; nextIndex becomes 5.
prev = (4, t3): entry 4 also has term 2. Reject; nextIndex becomes 4.
prev = (3, t2): match. By the Log Matching Property the follower now agrees with the leader on entries 1 to 3, so it deletes its conflicting entries 4 and 5 and appends the leader's 4 to 6.

blocks.md: The paper describes an optional speed-up: on rejection the follower returns the term of the conflicting entry and the first index it stores for that term, so the leader skips a whole term per round trip instead of one entry. The authors doubt it matters much in practice, since failures are rare.

The leader also tracks `matchIndex` per follower: the highest index known to be replicated there. The commit rule from the paper's Figure 2: if some N > commitIndex is stored on a majority (counting the leader) **and** `log[N].term == currentTerm`, set commitIndex = N. Because the leader's entry terms never decrease along its log, it is enough to test the majority index, as the code below does. Followers learn the commit point from the `leaderCommit` field and set their commitIndex to min(leaderCommit, index of their last new entry).

blocks.title: How a leader advances commitIndex
blocks.code:
def maybe_commit(match, terms, term, commit):
    # match[i]: highest index known stored on server i
    # (the leader counts its own last index)
    s = sorted(match, reverse=True)
    n = s[len(match) // 2]   # stored on a majority
    if n > commit and terms[n] == term:
        commit = n           # also commits 1..n
    return commit

# 5 servers, leader in term 3, entry terms by index:
terms = [None, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
print(maybe_commit([7, 7, 5, 4, 3], terms, 3, 2))
print(maybe_commit([7, 4, 4, 2, 1], terms, 3, 2))

scenes.caption: The leader's log has 7 entries: indexes 1 and 2 from term 1, 3 and 4 from term 2, 5 to 7 from term 3. It is leader of term 3 with commitIndex 2.
First call: matchIndex values of the 5 servers. Sorting in descending order puts the value held by a majority at position 5 // 2 = 2.
s[2] = 5: servers holding 7, 7 and 5 all store index 5, which is 3 of 5. Entry 5 has term 3, the current term, so commitIndex jumps from 2 to 5, committing 3 and 4 along with it.
Second call: index 4 is stored on 3 of 5 servers, but entry 4 is from term 2. Counting replicas of an older-term entry is not allowed (lesson 5 shows why), so commitIndex stays 2.

blocks.md: Stored on a majority is not the same as committed. An entry from an *earlier* term can sit on a majority and still be erased by a later leader. Commitment is only decided by counting replicas of an entry from the leader's *current* term, which then commits everything before it.

blocks.question: A 5-server cluster's leader is in term 3 with commitIndex 5. Its entries 6 to 9 all have term 3. The matchIndex values (leader included) are 9, 9, 8, 6, 5. What is the new commitIndex?
blocks.explain: Sorted descending: 9, 9, 8, 6, 5. The middle value 8 is stored on three servers (two with 9, one with 8), a majority of 5, and entry 8 has the current term. Index 9 is on only two servers. So commitIndex becomes 8, which also commits 6 and 7.

blocks.question: A follower's log has entries with terms [1, 1, 2] at indexes 1 to 3. It receives AppendEntries with prevLogIndex = 3, prevLogTerm = 3 and one new entry. What happens?
options: It appends the entry at index 4
It overwrites entry 3 with term 3 and appends
It rejects; the leader will retry with a smaller nextIndex
It starts an election because the leader looks stale
blocks.explain: The follower's entry 3 has term 2, not 3, so the consistency check fails and it refuses the request. The leader decrements nextIndex and retries until it finds the last index where both logs agree; only then are conflicting entries replaced.

lessons.title: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap

blocks.md:
Elections plus replication are not yet enough. Imagine a follower that was offline while the leader committed several entries. If it could become leader, it would force everyone's log to match its own and erase committed entries, and two state machines would apply different commands at the same index.

Raft prevents this with the **election restriction**: RequestVote carries the candidate's last log index and term, and a voter refuses its vote if its own log is **more up to date** than the candidate's.

blocks.caption: Compare the last entries: the later last term wins; with equal last terms, the longer log wins. Subscript c is the candidate, v the voter. The voter must also not have voted for someone else this term.

blocks.title: Why a new leader must hold every committed entry

scenes.caption: S1, leader of term T, commits an entry by storing it on S1, S2 and S3: a majority.
Later S5 runs for leader in some term U > T. It needs votes from a majority too, here S3, S4 and itself.

The two majorities must share a server, here S3. S3 holds the committed entry and only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, so S5 cannot win unless it holds the entry too.

blocks.md: This gives the **Leader Completeness Property**: a committed entry is present in the log of every later leader. The paper proves it by contradiction: take the first later leader missing the entry, and look at the voter shared by the commit majority and the vote majority. That voter held the entry and still voted, so the candidate's log was at least as up to date, which in both cases of the comparison above forces the candidate to hold the entry after all.

blocks.prompt: Look at state (c) of the next figure before playing it. S1 is leader of term 4 and its term-2 entry at index 2 is now stored on 3 of 5 servers. Is that entry committed?
blocks.reveal: **No.** In state (d) S5 can still be elected (its last term, 3, beats the voters' last terms, 2 or 1) and overwrite index 2. Being on a majority protects an entry only if it is from the current leader's term, because only then do the voters' logs end in a term no older candidate can beat.

blocks.title: The Figure 8 trap: a majority is not enough

scenes.caption: (a) S1 is leader in term 2 and has replicated its index-2 entry (term 2) only to S2. Cell values are entry terms.
(b) S1 crashes. S5 wins term 3 with votes from S3, S4 and itself (their logs end in term 1, not newer than S5's) and accepts a different entry at index 2.
(c) S5 crashes. S1 restarts, wins term 4, and resumes replication: its term-2 entry now sits on S1, S2 and S3, a majority. S1 also has a new term-4 entry at index 3.
(d) If S1 crashes now, S5 can win term 5 with votes from S2, S3, S4: its last term 3 beats their last term 2 or 1. It overwrites index 2 everywhere. The entry that sat on a majority is gone.
(e) Instead, suppose S1 first gets its term-4 entry onto S2 and S3. That entry is from S1's current term and on a majority, so it is committed, and index 2 commits with it.
In (e) S5 can no longer win: S1, S2 and S3 end in term 4, newer than S5's term 3, so they refuse their votes and S5 can gather at most 2.

blocks.md: A Raft leader commits by counting replicas **only** for entries from its own current term. Older entries become committed indirectly, when a later current-term entry after them commits. Entries keep their original term number forever, which is why this rule is needed.

Together these rules give Raft's five guarantees (Figure 3 of the paper):

1. **Election Safety**: at most one leader per term.
2. **Leader Append-Only**: a leader never overwrites or deletes its own entries.
3. **Log Matching**: same index and term means identical logs up to that point.
4. **Leader Completeness**: committed entries appear in all later leaders' logs.
5. **State Machine Safety**: no two servers apply different commands at the same index.

blocks.question: A voter's last log entry is (index 7, term 3). A candidate's last entry is (index 9, term 2). Does the voter grant its vote?
options: Yes, because the candidate's log is longer
No, because the voter's last term is higher
Yes, if the candidate's term number is higher than the voter's current term
Only if a majority already voted for the candidate
blocks.explain: Up to date is decided first by the last entry's term, and only by length when the terms are equal. Term 3 beats term 2, so the voter's log is more up to date and it refuses, however long the candidate's log is. A higher election term does not override this check.

blocks.question: A new leader is elected in term 6. Its log ends with entries from term 5 that are on a majority but not known to be committed, and no client requests arrive. What lets it learn which of those entries are committed?
options: Nothing: it must wait for the next client write
Counting replicas of the term-5 entries, since they are on a majority
Asking followers for their commitIndex and taking the maximum
Appending and committing a no-op entry in term 6
blocks.explain: Older-term entries cannot be committed by counting replicas. The paper has each new leader commit a blank no-op entry at the start of its term; once that term-6 entry commits, every entry before it is committed too. This matters for reads, as lesson 6 shows.

lessons.title: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts

blocks.md: **Clients.** Clients send every request to the leader; a follower that gets one replies with the address of the leader it last heard from. A leader may crash after committing a command but before replying, so the client retries and the command could run twice. The paper's fix: clients tag each command with a unique serial number, and the state machine remembers the latest serial number and response per client, answering duplicates without re-executing them.

scenes.caption: The client asks the leader to read x. The leader has already committed its term's no-op, so its commitIndex is current. It records readIndex = commitIndex, here 42.
The leader might have been deposed without knowing it. So it sends a round of heartbeats and waits for a majority to acknowledge.
F1 acknowledges. With itself, the leader has 2 of 3: no newer leader existed when it sent the heartbeats, so 42 was the highest commit index in the cluster.
Once its state machine has applied at least index 42, the leader reads x locally and replies. No log write and no disk sync were needed.

blocks.md: etcd's Raft library (used by etcd and CockroachDB, among others; TiKV uses raft-rs, a Rust port of it) exposes exactly this choice: `ReadOnlySafe`, the default and suggested option, communicates with a quorum; `ReadOnlyLeaseBased` relies on the leader lease, can be affected by clock drift, and requires `CheckQuorum`, which makes a leader step down when it has not heard from a quorum for an election timeout.

blocks.question: A team switches to lease-based reads to cut read latency. Under which condition can a client now see stale data?
options: When a follower's disk is slow
When the old leader's clock runs slow, so it keeps serving reads after a new leader has been elected
When two clients read the same key at once
Never; leases are as safe as ReadIndex
blocks.explain: A lease assumes the leader's sense of elapsed time matches the followers'. If its clock is slow or the process pauses, it may believe the lease is still valid after followers have timed out and elected someone else, and serve stale data. ReadIndex avoids this by checking with a majority on every batch of reads.

blocks.md: **Membership changes.** Replacing servers must not create a moment where two majorities do not overlap. Switching every server from the old configuration to the new one directly is unsafe, because servers switch at different times:

blocks.title: Switching configurations directly allows two leaders

scenes.caption: The cluster grows from {S1, S2, S3} to {S1 to S5}. Servers learn the new configuration at different times: right now S3, S4 and S5 use the new one, while S1 and S2 still use the old one.
S1 is elected with votes from S1 and S2: a majority (2 of 3) of the old configuration as S1 sees it.

In the same term S5 is elected with votes from S3, S4 and S5: a majority (3 of 5) of the new configuration. The two majorities do not overlap, so there are two leaders. Raft's fixes: joint consensus, or one server at a time.

blocks.md: The Raft paper uses **joint consensus**: the cluster first moves to a transitional configuration in which elections and commitment need separate majorities of *both* the old and the new sets, and only then moves to the new set. Ongaro's thesis later recommends a simpler rule: add or remove **one server at a time**, because any majority of the old set then overlaps any majority of the new set. New servers first join as non-voting members until their logs catch up.

**Timeouts.** The paper's timing requirement is broadcastTime much smaller than electionTimeout, which is much smaller than MTBF (mean time between failures of one server). Broadcast time is about 0.5 to 20 ms depending on storage, so the election timeout is likely 10 to 500 ms. In etcd's library time is counted in ticks: it suggests `ElectionTick = 10 * HeartbeatTick` and randomizes each timeout between `ElectionTick` and `2 * ElectionTick - 1` ticks.

blocks.title: How randomization range affects election collisions

y.label: P(second timer within d of first)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: n followers draw timeouts uniformly over a range of width R; a collision means a second timer fires less than d after the first, before the first candidate's RequestVote arrives. Risk is 1 - (1 - d/R)^n.

When R is smaller than d, timers always collide, which is the fixed-timeout case. Widening R from 50 to 150 ms cuts the risk from about 0.59 to 0.24. A collision only risks a split vote; it is not always one.
Slower disks or networks (larger d) push the curve up. That is why the election timeout must be much larger than the broadcast time.
More racing followers (a 9-server cluster has 8) also raise the risk. Randomness keeps it bounded rather than at 1.

blocks.md: **Disruptive servers.** A server cut off from the others keeps timing out and raising its term. When it reconnects, its high term forces the healthy leader to step down. The **Pre-Vote** extension from Ongaro's thesis (etcd: `PreVote`) has a would-be candidate first ask whether a majority would vote for it; servers that recently heard from a leader say no, so the isolated server never increments its term.

blocks.question: With Pre-Vote enabled, a server returns after 10 minutes in a network partition. What happens to the current leader?
options: It steps down because the returning server has a much higher term
It must run a new election to admit the server
Nothing: the server never raised its term while isolated, and returns to follower when the leader's heartbeat reaches it
It is removed from the cluster configuration
blocks.explain: While partitioned, the server could not get pre-votes from a majority, so it never incremented its term. On reconnecting, the other servers are still hearing heartbeats and refuse its pre-vote; once the leader's heartbeat reaches it, it settles as a follower in the same term.

blocks.md:
**Raft vs Paxos.** Both rely on overlapping majorities and both cost one round trip to a majority per command in steady state. The differences are in structure:

- Paxos is built from single-value instances; leadership is a liveness optimization, and a log can have gaps filled later with no-ops.
- Raft makes the leader central: the election is the first phase, entries flow only from leader to followers, and logs have no holes.
- Raft only elects candidates that already hold all committed entries, so a new leader never needs to fetch missing entries.

In a user study across two universities, 33 of 41 participants said Raft would be easier to implement and to explain.

Consensus is safe without any timing assumptions; timing only buys availability. Every production feature here (reads, reconfiguration, Pre-Vote) is checked against the same question: can two majorities that do not overlap make conflicting decisions?
